mediaItem.keyStats:
-   Official misconduct is a contributing factor in 46% of DNA exonerations (Innocence Project of Minnesota study).
-   Police suppressed evidence in over one-third of the first 74 exoneration cases.
-   9% of exoneration cases involved police coercing witnesses.
-   Around 24 conviction review units exist in the US (as of podcast recording time, likely around 2018 or later).
-   Dallas County went from the highest execution rate to the highest exoneration rate after establishing a conviction integrity unit.
mediaItem.itemTitle: Jason Flom and Barry Scheck with Barry Gibbs
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of Wrongful Conviction features the story of Barry Gibbs, who was wrongfully convicted of murder and served almost two decades in prison due to coerced eyewitness testimony orchestrated by a corrupt NYPD detective, Louis Eppolito. Eppolito, later revealed to be a Mafia hitman, framed Gibbs to protect the actual suspect. The episode includes interviews with Barry Gibbs, Barry Scheck (co-founder of the Innocence Project), and Vanessa Potkin (Innocence Project lawyer). They discuss the egregious misconduct in Gibbs' case, highlighting systemic issues like police corruption, prosecutorial overreach, inadequate defense, and problems with evidence handling. The conversation also touches upon the broader issue of wrongful convictions, the importance of conviction integrity units, and the need for prosecutorial accountability.  Barry Gibbs' exoneration came after the exposure of Eppolito's crimes, showcasing a rare instance of justice in a deeply flawed system. The episode ends with a call to support the Innocence Project.

featuredIndividual.caseLocation: Brooklyn, New York City, New York, USA
featuredIndividual.exonerationYear: Around 2004/2005 (inferred from newspaper article discovery in 2004 mentioned in transcript leading to reinvestigation and eventual exoneration).
featuredIndividual.timeServed: Almost two decades (approximately 19 years according to transcript mentioning 19 years served before end of podcast).
contributingFactorsRaw: Police misconduct (detective Louis Eppolito framed Gibbs).
Prosecutorial misconduct (implicitly, by relying on false evidence).
Possible inadequate original defense (not explicitly detailed in transcript but implied by focus on Innocence Project's later work).
organizationsInvolvedRaw: US Attorney's Office (Eastern District of New York, for reinvestigation)
innocenceLawyersRaw: Barry Scheck: Co-founder of the Innocence Project.
Vanessa Potkin: Director of Post-Conviction Litigation for the Innocence Project, long-serving lawyer with the Innocence Project.
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: A woman was strangled and her body was dumped from a car on the Bell Parkway in Brooklyn, New York City in 1986.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: False eyewitness testimony from Peter Mitchell, a jogger, who was coerced by Detective Louis Eppolito to identify Barry Gibbs.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes: Transcript does not provide details about the original trial defense lawyer's actions or inactions, only Barry Gibbs' distrust of the system and his lawyer's advice to provide hair samples for DNA.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Exposure of Detective Louis Eppolito as a corrupt "Mafia Cop" involved in murders for organized crime.
Discovery of the original NYPD case file in Eppolito's apartment in Las Vegas.
Retraction of false eyewitness testimony by Peter Mitchell, who confessed to being coerced by Eppolito.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: The transcript mentions the description of the perpetrator initially matched someone who worked at a chop shop in Brooklyn and was known to the cops. This individual showed up at the precinct with dyed hair and a lawyer shortly after the crime, but this lead was not pursued by Eppolito. The actual perpetrator is not explicitly named or definitively identified in the transcript, but suspicion is strongly implied to fall on this chop shop worker.

keyQuotesRaw: Jason Flom: "Yours is, as I was saying to Barry before, it's like the triple crown of malfeasance. You had jailhouse sniches, you have a police and prosecutorial misconduct. And then you have a situation where they either can't find or won't, or won't turn over the evidence that could have exonerated you long before you're two decades in prison."
Barry Gibbs: "I woke up and my life was never the same again. Cops came out with guns drawn and I never saw freedom ever ever since after that."

Barry Gibbs: "You broke my heart, you really did, you guys broke my heart. I made a sedimentary plot, a life insurance policy." (referring to the Innocence Project initially having to consider closing his case due to lack of physical evidence).

Peter Mitchell (jogger): "I've been waiting, you know, 20 years, I'm getting the chills right now for somebody to say this to me." (upon being approached by DEA agents and confessing to being coerced).
Barry Scheck: "To say corrupt is the understatement of all time. Louis Eppolito was working at this point in time for a crime family in New York City."
Vanessa Potkin on prosecutors: "When you're a prosecutor, you completely dehumanize the person who's accused, you know, that's how you do your job."

Barry Gibbs (final thoughts): "I've been through therapy. I've, you know, I've, I've been through a lot just to survive. I mean, I was in the hospital. I was messed up. I thought I was going to die. I'm here. I've been saved. I don't know why. I've got angels around me if I need a parking spot. It's there for me, you know, like, I don't know what it is, you know what I'm saying. And those are my angels that are, those are my angels that are around me. But the Innocence Project to me is more than just a family. There are hearts, you know. There are hearts."
systemicIssuesRaw: Problems with evidence handling and storage in crime labs.
Lack of accountability for prosecutorial misconduct.
Cognitive bias in the justice system, leading to dehumanization of defendants.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Need for stronger defense systems and better-funded defense lawyers.
Need for better systems of prosecutorial accountability, including potential criminal prosecution for deliberate misconduct and stronger bar discipline.
Reevaluation of how prosecutors are evaluated, shifting focus from convictions to justice.
Encouraging prosecutors to reinvestigate cases when exculpatory evidence emerges and to establish conviction integrity units.
Amending statutes of limitations to allow for federal prosecution of prosecutorial misconduct even after five years.
Improving evidence handling and storage procedures in crime labs.
Call to support the Innocence Project through donations and involvement.
personalNarrativeRaw: Barry Gibbs describes his life before wrongful conviction as the "American dream."
He recounts the trauma of arrest and imprisonment, highlighting the emotional and psychological toll of wrongful conviction.
He expresses deep gratitude and considers the Innocence Project as family, emphasizing their "hearts."
He describes his survival and current state as miraculous, attributing it to "angels."
His story is presented as deeply emotional and impactful, emphasizing the human cost of wrongful convictions.
additionalResourcesRaw: Book: "Mafia Cop" by Louis Eppolito (ironically, about Eppolito's supposed heroics before his exposure).
Book: "The Good Rat" by Jimmy Breslin, about Louis Eppolito case, which includes Barry Gibbs' story.
Movie: "Goodfellas" (Eppolito appeared in the first scene).
